results.what: Table of equatorial rectangular solar (or terrestrial) coordinates at unit (10^-4) radius scale, tabulated at equal steps of 1 grad of mean anomaly (400 steps per orbit), with e≈0.01679, ε≈23°27'52'', perigee ≈279.6°
results.modern_name: Solar ephemeris in rectangular equatorial coordinates (Keplerian solar orbit) tabulated by mean anomaly
results.usually_credited_to: Standard astronomical practice (solar tables of Lacaille, Delambre, von Zach, etc.)

results.what: Use of centesimal (grad) division of mean anomaly as tabular argument, suggesting equal-spacing quadrature over the Earth's orbit
results.modern_name: Equally spaced sampling for mechanical quadrature / averaging over an orbit
results.usually_credited_to: Common in perturbation computations; Gauss's own perturbation work (Pallas) is known

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine computed table of the Sun's or Earth's rectangular coordinates. The only mildly notable feature is the 400-part (grad) division of mean anomaly, which hints at a quadrature or averaging computation. Nothing here is mathematically non-standard.

checkable.asserts: Obliquity implied by Z/Y is about 23.4645 degrees (23°27'52'')
Z/Y is constant (about 0.434073) across the page

At mean anomaly 80 grads, r≈9950.7, matching sqrt(9886.673^2+1033.677^2+448.692^2) from the previous page
With X(179) corrected to 1524.903 the second differences are smooth (about -0.43, -0.40, -0.36, -0.32, -0.29 in sign convention)
With X(193) = -631.820 instead of -631.871 the second differences of X near the solstice become smooth
